title: Slavery in the law, honestly
hook: the books that say love your neighbor also regulate slavery; some laws limit it, some are hard to read, and Christians read them in different ways

segments.voice: Yesterday, Balaam's donkey, who saw the angel her master couldn't. Your line was even a donkey can see. Today, something many readers would rather not see: some of the hardest pages in the law. Day four hundred six.

A teenager posts a question online: why does the Bible allow slavery? The replies pile up. Some explain it away. Some defend it. The reply with the most votes says only that it's disturbing to watch people justify it. And the question itself barely gets answered. So here it is, straight. The laws of Moses, the same books that say love your neighbor as yourself and proclaim liberty in the jubilee, also regulate slavery. Today's word is the Hebrew for servant, or slave.
screen: `WHY DOES THE BIBLE ALLOW SLAVERY?` → `EXPLAINED AWAY, OR DEFENDED.` → `SO HERE IT IS, STRAIGHT.`

segments.voice: Ebed. In Hebrew it can mean servant, worker or slave, and the context decides. Moses himself is called the ebed of the LORD. But in these laws it often means a person owned by another. Some of the laws limit it. In the King James Bible: "If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve: and in the seventh he shall go out free." He's to be sent off with gifts, and the reason is given: "thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt." Another law forbids handing an escaped slave back to his master. Kidnapping a person to sell carried the death penalty. Other laws are hard to read. Foreigners could be bought, and "they shall be your bondmen for ever." A master who beats a slave who survives a day or two goes unpunished, "for he is his money." Honest readers don't pretend that's gentle. So how do Christians read these pages? Some point to the ancient world, where slavery was everywhere, and see these laws as limits on it, a first step. Some point to Jesus, who said Moses allowed divorce "because of the hardness of your hearts," and read the slavery laws the same way: allowed, not blessed. Some say plainly that these laws reflect their writers' world, not God's will for any time. Jewish readers have their own long tradition of wrestling with them too. And in nineteenth-century America, both sides quoted the Bible. Defenders of slavery quoted these laws and Paul. Abolitionists quoted the kidnapping law, the image of God in every person, and Paul's "neither bond nor free." The same law that regulates the ebed begins with slaves in Egypt crying out, and being heard.
screen: `EBED: SERVANT, OR SLAVE.` · `IN THE SEVENTH HE SHALL GO OUT FREE.` · `FOR HE IS HIS MONEY.` · `BOTH SIDES QUOTED THE BIBLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't defend it, don't skip it. Settle, and breathe. Let one of today's hard lines sit in front of you: for he is his money. Don't explain it. Just let it be as hard as it is. Then bring to mind the people, in the ancient world and in later centuries, who lived under words like these. Hold them for a moment with respect. If you pray, you can bring the hard verse to God as it is, the way Israel cried out in Egypt. If you don't, simply stay honest with it. The bell holds the time.
Ebed. Hebrew for servant, or slave: the word in the laws that limit slavery, and in the laws that are hard to read.
Your line: read the hard parts honestly. No defending, no skipping. Day four hundred six.

howItsDone: Christians read the Old Testament's slavery laws in different ways: as limits on an ancient practice, as concessions to hardness of heart, or as human words of their time. Churches today teach that slavery is a grave wrong, and many point to the image of God in every person.

original.note: Hebrew: servant, worker or slave. Moses is called the ebed of the LORD (Deuteronomy 34:5).

trapdoor: what you thought: the Bible either clearly approves of slavery, or never mentions it.
what it means: the law regulates slavery. some laws limit it, some are hard to read, and Christians read them in different ways.

what a scholar hears: Hebrew ebed covers servant, vassal and slave; the Torah treats Hebrew debt-servants (Exodus 21; Deuteronomy 15) differently from foreign slaves (Leviticus 25:44–46), and Deuteronomy 23:15–16 forbids returning a runaway.

Confirm fairness, and that Jewish readers are not made a foil.
